The Skellam Distribution

Source: R/dskellam.r, R/dskellam.sp.r, R/pskellam.r, and 3 more
skellam.Rd

Density, distribution function, quantile function and random generation for the Skellam distribution, the distribution of the difference of two independent Poisson variables, together with saddlepoint approximations to the density and distribution function.

Usage

dskellam(x, lambda1, lambda2 = lambda1, log = FALSE)

dskellam.sp(x, lambda1, lambda2 = lambda1, log = FALSE)

pskellam(q, lambda1, lambda2 = lambda1, lower.tail = TRUE, log.p = FALSE)

pskellam.sp(q, lambda1, lambda2 = lambda1, lower.tail = TRUE, log.p = FALSE)

qskellam(p, lambda1, lambda2 = lambda1, lower.tail = TRUE, log.p = FALSE)

rskellam(n, lambda1, lambda2 = lambda1)

Arguments

x, q

Numeric vector of quantiles (integers for the pmf).

lambda1, lambda2

Numeric vectors of non-negative rates; lambda2 defaults to lambda1.

log, log.p

Logical; if TRUE, probabilities are given as log(p).

lower.tail

Logical; if TRUE (default), probabilities are \(P(X \le x)\), otherwise \(P(X > x)\).

p

Numeric vector of probabilities.

n

Number of observations; if length(n) > 1, the length is taken to be the number required.

Value

dskellam gives the (log) probability mass function, pskellam the (log) distribution function, qskellam the quantile function and rskellam generates random deviates (an integer vector). dskellam.sp and pskellam.sp give the saddlepoint approximations. Names of the first argument are kept.

Invalid lambda values return NaN with a warning; a zero rate is allowed and reduces the distribution to a (reflected) Poisson.

Details

If \(Y_1 \sim \mathrm{Poisson}(\lambda_1)\) and \(Y_2 \sim \mathrm{Poisson}(\lambda_2)\) are independent, then \(X = Y_1 - Y_2\) has the Skellam distribution with probability mass function $$P(X = x) = e^{-(\lambda_1+\lambda_2)} (\lambda_1/\lambda_2)^{x/2} I_{|x|}(2\sqrt{\lambda_1 \lambda_2}), \qquad x = \ldots, -1, 0, 1, \ldots$$ where \(I_\nu\) is the modified Bessel function of the first kind. The mean is \(\lambda_1 - \lambda_2\) and the variance \(\lambda_1 + \lambda_2\). (If \(Y_1\) and \(Y_2\) are correlated Poisson variables with means \(\mu_i\) and correlation \(\rho\), the difference is still Skellam, with \(\lambda_i = \mu_i - \rho\sqrt{\mu_1 \mu_2}\).)

All functions follow the conventions of the stats distribution functions: arguments are recycled to a common length (with a warning when the lengths are not multiples), missing values propagate, invalid rates and probabilities give NaN with a warning, a non-integer x has density 0 (with a warning), and qskellam returns the smallest integer \(x\) with \(P(X \le x) \ge p\) (for lower.tail = TRUE), so that qskellam(pskellam(x, ...), ...) recovers x.

Numerical methods. dskellam evaluates the log of the Bessel function directly, so that log = TRUE is finite and accurate for any input: through besselI where that is reliable, through the uniform asymptotic expansion for large orders, a stable downward recurrence for large arguments, and the power series where besselI underflows. The relative error is below \(10^{-12}\) for rates up to at least \(10^7\), and below \(10^{-9}\) for extremely unequal large rates such as \((10^6, 10^3)\). pskellam uses the non-central chi-square identity of Johnson (1959) through pchisq when \(\lambda_1 + \lambda_2 \le 10^4\), and otherwise, as well as in tails where pchisq underflows, sums the log-pmf directly toward the nearer tail, so that far tails are exact on the log scale. qskellam starts from a Cornish-Fisher approximation and searches the integers with pskellam. rskellam returns the difference of two rpois draws.

dskellam.sp and pskellam.sp are the second-order saddlepoint approximation to the pmf and the Lugannani-Rice approximation to the cdf with Butler's second continuity correction (Butler 2007). Their relative error is of order \(1/(\lambda_1+\lambda_2)^2\) and \(1/(\lambda_1+\lambda_2)\) respectively; they are provided for users who want the approximations themselves and are not used by dskellam or pskellam.

References

  • Butler, R. (2007) Saddlepoint Approximations with Applications, Cambridge University Press.

  • Johnson, N. L. (1959) On an extension of the connection between Poisson and \(\chi^2\) distributions. Biometrika 46, 352-362.

  • Johnson, N. L., Kotz, S., & Kemp, A. W. (1993) Univariate Discrete Distributions, 2nd ed., John Wiley and Sons.

  • Olver, F. W. J. et al. (eds.) NIST Digital Library of Mathematical Functions, Section 10.41 (uniform asymptotic expansions of Bessel functions). https://dlmf.nist.gov/10.41

  • Skellam, J. G. (1946) The frequency distribution of the difference between two Poisson variates. Journal of the Royal Statistical Society, Series A 109(3), 296.

  • Strackee, J. & van der Gon, J. J. D. (1962) The frequency distribution of the difference between two Poisson variates. Statistica Neerlandica 16(1), 17-23.

See also

skellam.fit and skellam.reg for estimation; dpois for the Poisson distribution.

Examples

# Compare with Poisson when one lambda = 0
dskellam(0:10, 5, 0)
#>  [1] 0.006737947 0.033689735 0.084224337 0.140373896 0.175467370 0.175467370
#>  [7] 0.146222808 0.104444863 0.065278039 0.036265577 0.018132789
dpois(0:10, 5)
#>  [1] 0.006737947 0.033689735 0.084224337 0.140373896 0.175467370 0.175467370
#>  [7] 0.146222808 0.104444863 0.065278039 0.036265577 0.018132789

# Both lambdas non-zero
dskellam(c(-1,1), c(12,10), c(10,12))
#> [1] 0.0697968 0.0697968
pskellam(c(-1,0), c(12,10), c(10,12))
#> [1] 0.2965079 0.7034921

# Quantile function inverts the distribution function
qskellam(c(0.05, 0.95), 3, 4)
#> [1] -5  3
qskellam(pskellam(-3:3, 3, 4), 3, 4)
#> [1] -3 -2 -1  0  1  2  3

# Log-scale values stay finite far in the tails and at large rates
dskellam(500, 3, 2, log = TRUE)
#> [1] -2067.012
pskellam(0, 1e6, 1e6)
#> [1] 0.500141

# Random generation
set.seed(1)
rskellam(10, 8.5, 10.25)
#>  [1]  0 -2 -1 -5 -6  5  5  1  1 -6
